result.lens: The "root collapse" rule (deepdiff threshold_to_diff_deeper = 0.33) for dict-vs-dict diffs in test12_executable
result.verdict: RULE HOLDS. No counterexample found after ~120 binary invocations covering ~700 individual pair observations (6 pairs per run whose key counts can differ, plus 4 equal-key-set pairs). The candidate rule — COLLAPSE iff max(n1,n2) > 1 AND min(n1,n2)/max(n1,n2) < 0.33 (IEEE double, strict less-than) — predicted every observed outcome exactly, including the tightest rational boundaries around 0.33 (32/97, 33/100, 65/197, 67/203, 34/103, 330/1000, 659/2000, 661/2000), the union-size-1 guard (0 vs 1 keys), negative b/d, both asymmetric orders (b<d and b>d), and value-independence (a/c had zero effect on collapse). Equal-key-set pairs (r4/r5/r7/r10) never collapsed in any run.

findings.claim: Threshold is exactly the double 0.33 with STRICT less-than: ratio == 0.33 exactly does NOT collapse. b=33,d=100 gives 33/100 which rounds to the same double as the literal 0.33, so 0.33 < 0.33 is false -> per-key diff.

rulesForImplementer: Normalize sizes first: nb = Math.max(b, 0), nd = Math.max(d, 0). range() of a negative/zero count yields an empty dict, and negative b/d behave identically to 0.
Key counts per printed pair: r1=(nb,nd), r2=(nd,nb), r3=(nb,nd), r4=(nb,nb), r5=(nd,nd), r6=(nb,nd), r7=(nb,nb), r8=(0,nb), r9=(nd,0), r10=(nb,nb).

Collapse predicate (verified, use exactly this): function collapses(n1,n2){ const inter=Math.min(n1,n2), uni=Math.max(n1,n2); return uni > 1 && (inter/uni) < 0.33; }  Use the literal 0.33 and strict `<` — do NOT use <=, do NOT use 1/3, and do NOT rationalize (e.g. 100*inter < 33*uni) because 33/100, 66/200, 99/300 and 330/1000 must all evaluate as NOT-collapsing while 32/97 and 65/197 must collapse. Plain double division against the 0.33 literal reproduces this exactly.

The `uni > 1` guard is load-bearing: n1=0,n2=1 (and 1,0) must NOT collapse even though the ratio 0/1 = 0 is below the threshold. Those cases print per-key dictionary_item_added / dictionary_item_removed.
Equal key counts (r4, r5, r7, r10, and any r1/r2/r3/r6 where nb==nd) never collapse — ratio is 1. Emit per-key values_changed, or `{}` if every value matches.

Collapsed output is exactly one line: {'values_changed': {'root': {'new_value': <repr(t2)>, 'old_value': <repr(t1)>}}} — 'new_value' key first, then 'old_value'; path is the bare string 'root' in single quotes, never a bracketed path.

Dict repr inside a collapse is the full untruncated Python repr with keys in INSERTION order '0','1',...,'n-1' (i.e. '9' then '10' then '11', never lexicographic sort), format: {'0': 0, '1': -4, ...} with `': '` after each single-quoted key and `, ` between entries. Empty dict is `{}`. Never truncate — a 1000-key dict yields an 11842-char line.

Per-key (non-collapsed) output: top-level keys appear in the order dictionary_item_added, dictionary_item_removed, values_changed (only whichever are non-empty; with these nested-prefix key sets at most one of added/removed can be present). Path strings contain single quotes so Python repr wraps them in double quotes: "root['3']". Path lists and values_changed entries are in insertion order of the source dict, so "root['9']" precedes "root['10']".

If the two operands are fully equal (same keys and same values) the line is exactly `{}` — this is reached whenever nb==nd and no value differs (e.g. a==0 makes obj1==obj3, so r4 prints {}); r7 and r10 are always `{}`.
Collapse depends only on key counts, never on the integer values, so `a` and `c` must not enter the collapse decision.

result.lens: Exact output text: top-level key ordering, list/dict member ordering, and Python repr formatting of the 10 printed DeepDiff results
result.verdict: Output is fully deterministic (identical md5 across repeated runs — no hash-order randomness). Top-level keys always appear in the fixed canonical order dictionary_item_added, dictionary_item_removed, values_changed (only ever 6 shapes observed; added+removed can NEVER co-occur because the two key sets are always range() prefixes, so one is a subset of the other — 0 hits in a 360-line sweep). All list/dict members are in INSERTION (ascending numeric) order, never lexicographic: ["root['9']", "root['10']", "root['11']"] and ..."root['99']"..."root['100']"..."root['1004']". values_changed keeps insertion order with unchanged keys simply omitted (e.g. '9' followed directly by '11'). Rendering is plain Python dict repr: ", " separators, ": " after keys, "root['N']" double-quoted (contains ' and no "), bare 'root' single-quoted, {} for empty dict, new_value always before old_value, ints in full arbitrary precision. Exactly 10 lines, one "\n" per print, nothing on stderr, exit 0. Separately confirmed (affects which text form is emitted): a whole-root collapse to {'values_changed': {'root': {...}}} happens iff len(t1_keys | t2_keys) > 1 AND len(intersection)/len(union) < 0.33 (0.33 exactly does NOT collapse).

rulesForImplementer: Render each of the 10 results as a Python dict repr on its own line, terminated by exactly one \n (process.stdout.write(line + '\n')). Total 10 lines, no trailing blank line, nothing on stderr, exit 0.
Empty result prints exactly the two characters {} .

Top-level key emission order is FIXED and independent of computation order: dictionary_item_added, then dictionary_item_removed, then values_changed. Omit any key whose collection is empty. (type_changes and all iterable_* keys are unreachable in this program: all values are ints and both sides are always dicts.)

dictionary_item_added and dictionary_item_removed can never both appear, because the key sets are always range(b)/range(d)/empty, i.e. one is always a subset of the other. Do not write code that emits both.

Render dictionary_item_added/removed as a Python list: '[' + items.join(', ') + ']', items in ASCENDING NUMERIC order of the integer key (insertion order), NOT lexicographic. E.g. ["root['9']", "root['10']", "root['11']"] and ["root['98']", "root['99']", "root['100']", ...]. Single element: ["root['0']"].

Render values_changed as a Python dict: '{' + entries.join(', ') + '}' where each entry is <pathRepr> + ': ' + "{'new_value': " + repr(new) + ", 'old_value': " + repr(old) + '}'. new_value ALWAYS first. Iterate the intersected keys in ascending numeric order and SKIP keys whose values are equal (skipped keys leave no gap marker: ..."root['9']": {...}, "root['11']": {...}...).

String repr rule: a path like root['10'] contains a single quote and no double quote, so Python renders it double-quoted with no escaping: "root['10']". The bare path root has no quotes, so it renders single-quoted: 'root'. Dict keys inside the collapsed full-dict repr are digit strings rendered single-quoted: '0', '10', '1004'.
Separators are exactly ', ' between items/entries and ': ' after every key. No space after '{' or '[' and none before '}' or ']'.

Whole-root collapse (determines the text shape): let I = |t1keys ∩ t2keys|, U = |t1keys ∪ t2keys|. If U > 1 and I/U < 0.33 (strictly less; 33/100 = 0.33 does NOT collapse), emit only {'values_changed': {'root': {'new_value': <repr of t2>, 'old_value': <repr of t1>}}} and no added/removed keys. Otherwise do the per-key diff. Note U == 1 (e.g. {} vs a 1-key dict) never collapses.

In the collapsed form print the FULL dict repr of each side with keys in insertion (ascending numeric) order, never sorted or truncated: {'0': 0, '1': 1, ..., '10': 10, ...}; the empty side prints as {} . This holds for arbitrarily large dicts (verified past key '1000').

Integers must be exact arbitrary-precision decimals (use BigInt in Node): i*a, i*a*2, i*c, i*c+10 can exceed 2^53 (e.g. --a 123456789012345678 yields 493827156049382712). Negative values print with a leading '-'. Never emit float formatting or exponent notation.
b <= 0 (and d <= 0) means an empty dict via range(); DeepDiff({}, {}) prints {} .

Argparse errors: print nothing to stdout, write 'usage: <prog> [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D\n<prog>: error: the following arguments are required: --d\n' (listing every missing option, comma-separated, in --a/--b/--c/--d order) to stderr, exit 2, where <prog> is the basename of argv[0].
counterexamples: Lexicographic ordering hypothesis REFUTED: b=9,d=12 gives ["root['9']", "root['10']", "root['11']"], not ["root['10']", "root['11']", "root['9']"].

Sorted-values_changed hypothesis REFUTED: a=1,c=1,b=110,d=110 line 3 runs ..."root['99']"..., "root['100']"..., "root['101']"... consecutively and omits "root['10']" entirely; a lexicographic order would put '100' right after '10'/'1'.

'DeepDiff({}, X) always yields dictionary_item_added' REFUTED: with b=3 it yields {'values_changed': {'root': {'new_value': {'0': 0, '1': 1, '2': 2}, 'old_value': {}}}} (threshold collapse), but with b=1 it yields {'dictionary_item_added': ["root['0']"]} (union size 1 guard).
'ratio < 0.33 or <= 0.33' ambiguity resolved: b=33,d=100 (exactly 0.33) does NOT collapse (added list printed), while b=32,d=100 does collapse.

result.lens: CLI surface (argparse) and Python int() coercion semantics of /workspace/dataset/test12_executable
result.verdict: Fully characterized. The binary is a PyInstaller onefile of CPython 3.12 (libpython3.12.so.1.0) running stock argparse.ArgumentParser() with four required `type=int` long options. prog = basename(argv[0]) (dynamic, NOT hardcoded "test12_executable"). Help -> stdout, exit 0, 142 bytes. All CLI errors -> stderr, exit 2, always exactly two lines (wrapped usage line + "PROG: error: MSG"). Integer coercion is exact Python int(str): Unicode-whitespace strip, optional ASCII sign, Unicode Nd digits (any script, mixable), single underscores strictly between digits, arbitrary precision (verified up to 4300 digits), 0x/0b/0o/1e3/1.5/','-forms rejected. Two non-argparse failure modes exist: exit 1 with a traceback when any printed integer needs more than 4300 decimal digits, and prog-name/usage-wrap variance driven by argv[0] and $COLUMNS.

rulesForImplementer: PROG must be computed at runtime as basename(process.argv[1]) (the script/exe path as invoked), NOT the literal "test12_executable". Use it in both the "usage: PROG ..." line and the "PROG: error: ..." line.
USAGE_LINE (80-col default) is exactly: `usage: ${PROG} [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D`.

HELP (stdout, then exit 0) is exactly, with a trailing newline and no trailing blank line: `usage: ${PROG} [-h] --a A --b B --c C --d D

options:
  -h, --help  show this help message and exit
  --a A
  --b B
  --c C
  --d D
` (142 bytes for PROG="test12_executable"). Two leading spaces per entry; exactly two spaces between `-h, --help` and `show`.
Every parse error: write `${USAGE_LINE}\n${PROG}: error: ${MSG}\n` to STDERR, write NOTHING to stdout, exit code 2. Never wrap the error line.
MSG for missing required options: `the following arguments are required: ` + the missing option strings in declaration order a,b,c,d joined by `, `.

MSG for an option given with no following value (or whose next token is an option-looking token): `argument --X: expected one argument`, where --X is the canonical declared name (--a/--b/--c/--d), even if the user typed an abbreviation.

MSG for a value that fails int(): `argument --X: invalid int value: ` + pythonRepr(rawValue). pythonRepr: wrap in single quotes; if the value contains a `'` but no `"`, wrap in double quotes instead; escape backslash, \t, \n, \r and other C0 controls Python-style (\t, \n, \r, \xNN); emit all printable non-ASCII characters raw as UTF-8 (do NOT \u-escape).
MSG for extra tokens: `unrecognized arguments: ` + extras.join(' ') in input order (an empty-string extra therefore yields a trailing space).
MSG for `--help=V` or any abbreviation of it with `=`: `argument -h/--help: ignored explicit argument 'V'`.

Ordering of checks (left-to-right, argparse semantics): (1) walk tokens in order; `-h`/`--h`/`--he`/`--help` encountered => print HELP, exit 0 immediately; (2) an option whose value fails int() errors immediately, so it beats both missing-required and unrecognized; (3) after the walk, missing-required beats unrecognized-extras.

Token classification: an exact match on `-h`, `--help`, `--a`, `--b`, `--c`, `--d` wins. `--X=V` splits on the first `=`. Otherwise, for a `--`-prefixed token, do unique-prefix matching against {--help,--a,--b,--c,--d} (so `--h`, `--he`, `--hel`, `--help` all mean help; `--ab`, `--a5` match nothing). Single-dash tokens other than exactly `-h` never match. Unmatched tokens are extras. A token that is not option-like is: empty string, or does not start with `-`, or matches /^-\d+$|^-\d*\.\d+$/ (negative number), or contains a space — such tokens can be consumed as an option's value.

`--` handling: the first `--` is NOT silently dropped (there are no positionals to consume it). A `--` token makes every subsequent token a non-option (so later `--a 1` etc. are extras, and the required-args error fires); the `--` itself is reported as an extra when nothing follows/consumes it (`unrecognized arguments: --`).
Duplicate options: last occurrence wins (simple assignment).

int() port (return BigInt): (1) strip leading and trailing Unicode whitespace — must include space \t \n \v \f \r, U+001C-U+001F, U+0085, U+00A0, U+1680, U+2000-U+200A, U+2028, U+2029, U+202F, U+205F, U+3000; (2) optional single ASCII '+' or '-' (no other sign character, no whitespace after the sign); (3) then one or more Unicode DECIMAL digits (general category Nd, any script, scripts may be mixed) optionally separated by single `_` characters that must each sit strictly between two digits; (4) reject anything else — empty, `_1`, `1_`, `1__0`, `+ 7`, `+-5`, `1.5`, `1e3`, `0x10`, `0b101`, `0o7`, `3,4`, and non-Nd numerics (U+00B2 superscript, U+2162 roman numeral, U+2462 circled digit); (5) map each Nd code point to its decimal value (e.g. U+0661->1, U+0669->9, U+0966+n, U+FF10+n, U+1D7D8+n for double-struck) and accumulate as BigInt; leading zeros are fine (`007`->7n, `00`->0n, `-0`->0n).

Enforce the CPython 4300-digit int-string limit: if the parsed value has MORE than 4300 decimal digits (underscores excluded from the count), reject it as `invalid int value: <repr of the whole raw token>` with exit 2. Also, when serializing any integer for output, if its decimal representation would exceed 4300 digits, flush the lines printed so far to stdout and abort with exit code 1 and stderr `Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "test12.py", line <N>, in <module>
  File "deepdiff/diff.py", line 2007, in __str__
ValueError: Exceeds the limit (4300 digits) for integer string conversion; use sys.set_int_max_str_digits() to increase the limit
[PYI-<pid>:ERROR] Failed to execute script 'test12' due to unhandled exception!
` (the pid in the PYI line varies, and <N> is the source line of the failing print: 17,19,21,23,25,27,29,31,33,35 for r1..r10).

Usage/help wrapping width = (COLUMNS env var if it parses to an integer > 0, else 80) - 2. With the default 80 nothing wraps, so a fixed single-line usage is correct unless you want to replicate COLUMNS-driven wrapping (hanging indent of len('usage: '+PROG+' ') spaces, or a 7-space indent when the first chunk does not fit).
Success path: exit 0, exactly 10 lines on stdout each ending in \n, nothing on stderr. Non-positive --b/--d produce empty source dicts (range semantics), never an error.
counterexamples: `--a5` and `-x` alone do NOT produce "unrecognized arguments" — the missing-required error is emitted first because required-checking happens inside parse_known_args, before extras are reported.
A trailing `--` is not ignored: `--a 1 --b 2 --c 3 --d 2 --` fails with `unrecognized arguments: --` (exit 2) even though all four options are valid.

`--a -0x10` is NOT an invalid-int error but `argument --a: expected one argument`, because `-0x10` is option-like (starts with '-', not a negative number, no space) so it is never offered as the value.
`-h --a x` exits 0 with help, but `--a x -h` exits 2 with `invalid int value: 'x'` — help does not unconditionally win.
A value of 4300 nines parses fine but the program then dies with exit code 1 mid-output (only line 1 written) because 2*a needs 4301 digits.
Do not assume int() is ASCII-only: `--a ١٢` (U+0661 U+0662) is accepted as 12, and `--a 1٢` is accepted as 12.
